claim: Hamel Husain recommends appointing a single domain expert as a 'benevolent dictator' to make quality decisions, eliminating annotation conflicts and decision paralysis.
quote: appointing a single domain expert as a 'benevolent dictator' is the most effective approach ... a single expert eliminates annotation conflicts and prevents the paralysis

claim: When multiple annotators are used, the workflow is: draft a rubric with Pass/Fail definitions, label a shared set independently, measure Cohen's Kappa, then hold alignment sessions to reconcile disagreements and refine the rubric.
quote: Draft an initial rubric with clear Pass/Fail definitions ... Measure Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA) using a chance-corrected metric like Cohen's Kappa ... Facilitate alignment sessions to discuss disagreements and refine the rubric

claim: Binary pass/fail evaluations are preferred because they force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling, and you should write evaluators for errors you actually discover, not ones you imagine.
quote: Binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling ... Write evaluators for errors you discover, not errors you imagine

claim: For ground-truth labeling Hamel warns you must hand-validate each LLM-suggested label because LLM mistakes lead to unreliable benchmarks; LLMs can suggest categories but humans must review before adopting.
quote: For ground truth labeling...hand-validate each label. LLMs can make mistakes that lead to unreliable benchmarks ... use an LLM to suggest which categories apply to each new trace...Review these suggestions before adopting

claim: Shankar et al.'s EvalGen identifies 'criteria drift': users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs is what helps them define those criteria, so criteria cannot be fully fixed a priori.
quote: users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria ... some criteria appears dependent on the specific LLM outputs observed (rather than independent criteria that can be defined a priori)

claim: EvalGen aligns LLM-as-judge implementations to human preferences by asking humans to grade a subset of outputs and selecting candidate evaluators that best match those grades; LLM-generated evaluators otherwise inherit the LLM's own flaws.
quote: EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs; this feedback is used to select implementations that better align with user grades ... LLM-generated evaluators simply inherit all the problems of the LLMs they evaluate, requiring further human validation

claim: Standard chance-corrected inter-annotator agreement metrics are Cohen's Kappa, Fleiss' Kappa, and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, each suited to different annotation scenarios.
quote: Common statistical measures used to assess inter-annotator agreement include Cohen's Kappa, Fleiss' Kappa, and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, each suitable for different types of data and annotation scenarios.

claim: Cohen's kappa and Fleiss' kappa both correct for chance agreement; Cohen's handles two raters while Fleiss' generalizes to more than two, and reported kappa scores of 0.6-0.8 indicate substantial and above 0.8 almost-perfect agreement.
quote: Cohen's kappa designed for two raters while Fleiss' kappa generalizes the approach to settings with more than two raters ... strong agreement (0.6-0.8) to almost perfect agreement (> 0.8)

claim: LLM-as-judge exhibits self-preference bias rooted in perplexity: judges assign higher scores to lower-perplexity (more familiar) outputs than humans do, regardless of whether the model itself generated them.
quote: LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated.

claim: LLM judges carry systematic biases including verbosity bias (preferring longer responses) and position bias (favoring the option presented first), and can align more with lay-user preferences than with subject-matter-expert standards.
quote: verbosity bias (where longer responses receive higher scores regardless of quality), and position bias (where responses presented earlier are preferred) ... LLM judgement is often more closely aligned with lay user preferences than SME standards
